A '''Newey–West estimator''' is used in [[statistics]] and [[econometrics]] to provide an estimate of the [[covariance matrix]] of the parameters of a [[linear regression|regression-type]] model where the standard assumptions of [[regression analysis]] do not apply.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.mathfinance.cn/newey-west-estimator/|title=Newey West estimator – Quantitative Finance Collector|access-date=2009-05-18|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180624175743/http://www.mathfinance.cn/newey-west-estimator/|archive-date=2018-06-24}}</ref> It was devised by [[Whitney K. Newey]] and [[Kenneth D. West]] in 1987, although there are a number of later variants.<ref name="NeweyWest1987">{{Cite journal | doi = 10.2307/1913610 | last1 = Newey | first1 = Whitney K | last2 = West | first2 = Kenneth D | year = 1987 | title = A Simple, Positive Semi-definite, Heteroscedasticity and Autocorrelation Consistent Covariance Matrix | jstor = 1913610| journal = Econometrica | volume = 55 | issue = 3| pages = 703–708 | url = http://www.nber.org/papers/t0055.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.2307/2938229 | last1 = Andrews | first1 = Donald W. K. |author-link=Donald Andrews | year = 1991 | title = Heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent covariance matrix estimation | jstor = 2938229| journal = Econometrica | volume = 59 | issue = 3| pages = 817–858 | url = http://cowles.yale.edu/sites/default/files/files/pub/d08/d0877-r.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.2307/2297912 | last1 = Newey | first1 = Whitney K. | last2 = West | first2 = Kenneth D. | year = 1994 | title = Automatic lag selection in covariance matrix estimation | jstor = 2297912| journal = Review of Economic Studies | volume = 61 | issue = 4| pages = 631–654 | url = http://www.nber.org/papers/t0144.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Smith | first1 = Richard J. | year = 2005 | title = Automatic positive semidefinite HAC covariance matrix and GMM estimation | url = http://wrap.warwick.ac.uk/733/1/WRAP_Smith_Automatic_semidefinate.pdf| journal = Econometric Theory | volume = 21 | issue = 1| pages = 158–170 | doi = 10.1017/S0266466605050103 }}</ref> The estimator is used to try to overcome [[autocorrelation]] (also called serial correlation), and [[heteroskedasticity]] in the [[errors and residuals in statistics|error terms]] in the models, often for regressions applied to [[time series]] data.  The abbreviation "HAC," sometimes used for the estimator, stands for "heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent."<ref name="NeweyWest1987"/> There are a number of HAC estimators described in,<ref name=":0" /> and HAC estimator does not refer uniquely to Newey–West. One version of Newey–West Bartlett requires the user to specify the bandwidth and usage of the Bartlett kernel from [[Kernel density estimation]]<ref name=":0" />

Regression models estimated with time series data often exhibit autocorrelation; that is, the [[error term]]s are correlated over time. The [[Heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors|heteroscedastic consistent estimator]] of the error covariance is constructed from a term <math>X^{\operatorname{T}}\Sigma X</math>, where <math>X</math> is the [[design matrix]] for the regression problem and <math>\Sigma</math> is the covariance matrix of the residuals. The least squares estimator <math>b</math> is a [[consistent estimator]] of <math>\beta</math>. This implies that the [[least squares]] [[errors and residuals in statistics|residuals]] <math>e_i</math> are "point-wise" consistent estimators of their population counterparts <math>E_i</math>. The general approach, then, will be to use <math>X</math> and <math>e</math> to devise an estimator of <math>X^{\operatorname{T}}\Sigma X</math>.<ref>{{cite book |last=Greene |first=William H. |year=1997 |title=Econometric Analysis |url=https://archive.org/details/econometricanaly0000gree |url-access=registration |edition=3rd }}</ref> This means that as the time between error terms increases, the correlation between the error terms decreases. The estimator thus can be used to improve the [[ordinary least squares]] (OLS) [[Regression analysis|regression]] when the residuals are heteroscedastic and/or autocorrelated.

: <math> X^{\operatorname{T}}\Sigma X=\frac{1}{T} \sum^T_{t=1} e_t^2 x_t x^{\operatorname{T}}_t + \frac{1}{T} \sum^L_{\ell=1} \sum^T_{t=\ell+1} w_\ell e_t e_{t-\ell}(x_t x^{\operatorname{T}}_{t-\ell} + x_{t-\ell} x^{\operatorname{T}}_t) </math>

: <math>w_\ell=1 - \frac\ell {L+1}</math><!-- no definition for w, l or L -->

where ''T'' is the sample size, <math>e_t</math> is the <math>t^\text{th}</math> residual and <math>x_t</math> is the <math>t^\text{th}</math> row of the design matrix, and <math> w_\ell </math> is the Bartlett kernel <ref>{{Cite web |title=time series – Bartlett Kernel (Newey West Covariance Matrix) |url=https://stats.stackexchange.com/q/329513 |access-date=2022-09-15 |website=Cross Validated |language=en}}</ref> and can be thought of as a weight that decreases with increasing separation between samples. Disturbances that are farther apart from each other are given lower weight, while those with equal subscripts are given a weight of 1. This ensures that second term converges (in some appropriate sense) to a finite matrix. This weighting scheme also ensures that the resulting covariance matrix is [[Definite_symmetric_matrix|positive semi-definite]].<ref name="NeweyWest1987"/> ''L''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0 reduces the Newey–West estimator to [[Huber–White standard error]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Verallgemeinerte Kleinst-Quadrate-Schätzung |trans-title=Generalized Least Squares estimation |url=https://www.uni-kassel.de/fb07/index.php?eID=dumpFile&t=f&f=2817&token=d05ecfbfd0070bb022cff4d2384120b19ec2628e |website=www.uni-kassel.de|publisher=Uni-Kassel|access-date=2023-09-21}}</ref> ''L'' specifies the "maximum lag considered for the control of autocorrelation. A common choice for ''L''" is <math>T^{1/4}</math>.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=Greene |first=William H. |title=Econometric analysis |date=2012 |publisher=Pearson |isbn=978-0-273-75356-8 |edition=7th |location=Boston |oclc=726074601}}</ref>

== Software implementations ==
In [[Julia (programming language)|Julia]], the CovarianceMatrices.jl package <ref>{{cite web |title=CovarianceMatrices.jl package | url=https://github.com/gragusa/CovarianceMatrices.jl}} </ref> supports several types of heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent covariance matrix estimation including Newey–West, White, and Arellano.

In [[R (programming language)|R]], the packages <code>sandwich</code><ref name=":0">{{cite web |title=sandwich: Robust Covariance Matrix Estimators |work=CRAN |url=https://cran.r-project.org/package=sandwich }}</ref> and <code>plm</code><ref>{{cite web |title=plm: Linear Models for Panel Data |work=CRAN |url=https://cran.r-project.org/package=plm }}</ref> include a function for the Newey–West estimator.

In [[Stata]], the command <code>newey</code> produces Newey–West standard errors for coefficients estimated by OLS regression.<ref>{{cite web |title=Regression with Newey–West standard errors |work=Stata Manual |url=https://www.stata.com/manuals14/tsnewey.pdf }}</ref>

In [[MATLAB]], the command <code>hac</code> in the Econometrics toolbox produces the Newey–West estimator (among others).<ref>{{cite web |title=Heteroscedasticity and autocorrelation consistent covariance estimators |work=Econometrics Toolbox |url=https://www.mathworks.com/help/econ/hac.html}}</ref>

In [[Python (programming language)|Python]], the <code>statsmodels</code><ref>{{cite web |title=statsmodels: Statistics |work=statsmodels |url=http://www.statsmodels.org/dev/stats.html }}</ref> module includes functions for the covariance matrix using Newey–West.

In [[Gretl]], the option <code>--robust</code> to several estimation commands (such as <code>ols</code>) in the context of a time-series dataset produces Newey–West standard errors.<ref>{{cite web |title=Robust covariance matrix estimation |work=Gretl User's Guide, chapter 22 |url=https://gretl.sourceforge.net/gretl-help/gretl-guide.pdf }}</ref>

In [[SAS (software)|SAS]], the Newey–West corrected standard errors can be obtained in PROC AUTOREG and PROC MODEL <ref>{{cite web |title=Usage Note 40098: Newey–West correction of standard errors for heteroscedasticity and autocorrelation|url=http://support.sas.com/kb/40/098.html}} </ref>
